## Paper

## Abstract

Highly electrically conductive polymer composites are fundamental materials for today’s electronic engineering. However, these composites are very expensive since heavy loading of costly conductive particles (fillers) is required to guarantee high electrical conductivity. This work successfully reports that weak electromagnetic waves (EMWs) could cohere the microparticles to optimize conductive networks for highly conductive polymer composites. Such an EMW strategy arises from the earliest EMW detector (coherer) invented by Marconi and Popov in 1895 via the breakdown of surface oxides and cohering of the micro-conductors by EMWs. The flexible composite (metal microfiber-polymer) shows a unique insulator-conductor transition with drastic resistance change (50 MΩ to 1 kΩ) under weak EMWs (power: 10-6 mW). The EMW strategy is extremely rapid (0.34 µs) and highly stable (104 cycles). Such EMW effect universally describes the interactions between EM fields and composite materials that are suitable for general conductors (e.g., carbon- and metal-fillers) and most polymers.

---

## Introduction

Electrically conductive polymer composites are the fundamental materials in today’s electronic engineering and are broadly applied as soft conductors, plastic electronic components (e.g., antistatic shielding cover), and electronic packaging materials due to their combined advantages of electrical conductivity, polymer flexibility, and interfacial bonding capability1–3. The current market for conductive polymer composites achieves as high as $4.4 billion per year in the electronic industry4,5. Although broadly utilized, the highly conductive composites are usually quite expensive since very high loading of costly fillers (usually beyond 75wt% for noble metal particles) is required to achieve sufficient conductive networks to guarantee good electrical performance3. Lots of investigations have been performed to lower the loading values to reduce the cost, including using specific fillers (silver nanowires, silver flakes, carbon fibers, and graphene) and unique blending strategies (solvent or bicontinuous phase assisted)6–9. However, these techniques or specific fillers are not prevalent in the industry due to the difficult synthesis, complicated steps, and strict requirements for the processing. So far, using a large quantity of costly conductive fillers in polymers is the most favored industrial method in electronics for high electrical conductivity in composites.

Electromagnetic waves (EMWs) have been the undoubted foundation for human society for more than 140 years since Hertz’s discovery in the 1880s10,11. The study of the interactions between EMWs and conductors is an important aspect of electromagnetics, yielding fruitful results for today’s technologies12. For example, radio technology uses EMWs and conductors to transmit signals, serving as the foundation of modern communication disciplines and making significant contribution to human society13,14. In the early history of radio technology, both Marconi and Popov utilized the interaction between metal powders and EMWs to receive EMWs as the earliest radio signal detector (coherer) in 189515. Such interaction is called the Branly effect, in which the high electrical resistive metal powders could be conveniently turned into low resistive materials by cohering the metal particles upon weak EMWs16,17. Although the coherer-type radio detector was quickly replaced by other advanced detectors due to the stability issue, the phenomenon between metals and EMWs strongly reminds us of a promising and convenient strategy to obtain highly conductive composites by low-energy EMWs.

In this work, we revisit the oldest EMW detector (coherer) from over a century ago and report a universal and convenient strategy that can cohere the conductive microfillers in polymers for highly electrically conductive composites through weak EMWs. Such an EMW effect arises from the Branly effect that can break down the thin oxides and then produce the joule heat from the induced voltage by EMWs to cohere the microfillers in polymers. Excitingly, applying weak EMW (power: 10−6 mW) on the composites remotely for a very short time (<1 µs) is sufficient to optimize the conductive network in the composites, leading to a significant change in material performance. The flexible metal microfiber polymer composite can have a unique insulator-conductor transition with a drastic resistance change in 4 orders of magnitude from 50 MΩ to 1 kΩ through emitting EMWs at a long distance (5 m). Systematic investigations in this work find that the EMW effect is heavily influenced by the amplitude and the rising/falling edge time of EMWs. Remarkably, the resistance transition is completely reversible (recovery ratio: ~100%) upon external micro-force (29 mN) and can withstand more than 104 cycles of such transition. It is worth noting that the EMW effect is a general strategy that universally describes the interactions between dynamic EM fields and conductors without strict requirements for metals and polymers. Flexible resistive memory devices with similar behaviors to magnetoresistive materials can be successfully and conveniently fabricated based on EMW effects. More importantly, different from the phenomena observed by Marconi and Popov, this work creatively finds that cohering of microfillers via EMWs could be permanently locked in the polymer composites if further treated by joule heating via transient voltage, which provides the electronic industry with a convenient strategy for highly conductive composites.

---

## Results

The composite in this work is prepared by simple shear mixing of metal micro-conductors (metal microfiber) and polymers (Figs. S1, S2 and Table S1). Styrene-Isoprene-Styrene (SIS) rubber (Mw: 30 kDa) is used as the polymer matrix since it shows high extensibility, while the metal microfibers in the work are steel fibers (SAE 316L, diameter: 12 μm and length: 500–800 μm, shown in Fig. S3) that are utilized as micro-fillers in polymer composites. In this work, unless specified, the EM materials refer to steel microfiber-SIS composite using SIS as a polymer matrix with 15 wt% above steel fibers (Fig. S4). Figure 1a, b show that emitting EMWs for a short time on a single metal microfiber will induce a high voltage between fibers. The induced voltage is also monitored (approximately 20 V, Figs. 1c and S5) when emitting the EMWs by an electrical fast burst (EFB) generator (Fig. S6) with a rising edge at 8 ns. Such induced voltage could produce a strong electric field strength (2.2 × 107 V/m based on the simulation of COMSOL Multiphysics, Fig. S7) among the fibers, exceeding the dielectric breakdown threshold of copper oxide18. The power-frequency spectrum of the EMWs is also recorded by the real-time spectrum analyzer (Fig. S8), which shows that the weak EMWs (power: 10−6 mW, triggered by EFB or piezoelectric ignitor with a total energy below 75 μJ) are sufficient to cohere the microfiber. Figure 1d exhibits that when the metal microfibers form composite materials with polymers, the microscopic breakdown of the surface oxide of microfibers in the polymer matrix before and after the EMW treatment will optimize the conductive network of the materials. Importantly, the EMW effect can be a general strategy that universally describes the microscopic interactions between EMWs and conductors. Figures S9–S13 and Table S1 demonstrate that other common conductors (such as copper particles, copper fibers, and carbon) and general polymers such as polycarbonate (PC), styrene-ethylene-butylene-styrene (SEBS), thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), low-density polyethylene (LDPE), ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA), and polylactic acid (PLA) show similar EMW effects.

The mechanism of the EMW effect for composites can be demonstrated by an old phenomenon reported over one century ago called the Branly effect. The Branly effect was used to construct the earliest radio signal detector (coherer) by Marconi and Popov via cohering metal powders upon weak EMWs. As shown in Fig. 2a1–a4, and 3D microscopic images (Fig. 2a3), after EMW (τ = 4 ns, Fig. S14) treatment, tiny dents are observed on the points where the steel beads (SAE 316L, Φ: 10 mm) contact. It indicates that EMWs can generate sufficiently high voltage between the steel beads, which will break down the surface oxide and cohere the metals through the induced voltage. To clearly observe such a cohering effect, a 2 kV transient voltage (500 µs, Fig. S15) is applied to the ends of the string with four contact beads. Due to the surface oxides of the beads, the string is electrically insulating. As shown in Fig. 2b, visible electric spark is generated among the four beads under the transient voltage, and the resistance is reduced to 3.8 Ω immediately. The four beads are cohered together at their joints (Fig. 2c) due to the local joule heating without dropping off upon lifting (inset in Fig. 2c). Building on this, copper fibers are positioned 1 cm away from the EMW source and treated for 20 s. As shown in Fig. S16, after EMW treatment, the surface at the contact point of the metal fibers is disrupted, leading to cohered fibers. These experimental results directly demonstrate the breakdown of the surface oxide layer on the microfibers. To further verify the transient heat for the composite sample under induced low voltage, a transient voltage (80 V, 412 μs) is applied across the EM material, and the resulting thermal effects are observed by an infrared camera (Fig. S17). The surface oxide breakdown and joule heating offer the efficient EMW effect for conductive microfillers in polymer composites. In addition, the previous report19 and information from prototype experiments in this work (Fig. S18) illustrate the Branly effect for pure carbon and metal fillers. EMW induces the insulator-to-conductor transition primarily through localized oxide layer breakdown and removal at the metal. As shown in the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) mapping (Fig. S19), after EMW treatment, the reduction of the O element (from 50.01 to 10.32%) in the energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) image of the treated oxidized copper surface directly demonstrates the removal of the oxide layer. In addition, samples with copper particles whose oxide layer is removed (Fig. S20) exhibited no such EMW effects. The surface oxide breakdown and joule heating offer the efficient EMW effect for conductive microfillers in polymer composites.

Figure 2d provides an intuitive view of the conductive network optimization upon measuring the electrical conductivity of the materials. Interestingly, similar to radio technology, EMW effects can be applied remotely (Fig. 2d). When EMWs are emitted at different distances from the sample (Movies S1, S2 and Figs. S21, S23), EM materials will show a unique insulator-conductor transition immediately. When EMWs are emitted at a distance of 5 m from the EM material, the composite exhibit a dramatic reduction in electrical resistance from >50 MΩ to 1 kΩ, and the lighting of the light-emitting diode (LED) is observed (Figs. 2d and S21–S23). EM materials are placed at various distances (0–6.6 m) from the EMW source to further investigate the influence of the EMW source-to-material distance on the EMW effect. As shown in Fig. S24, the effect attenuates exponentially with increasing distance from the EMW source. High-temporal-resolution measurements obtained through oscilloscopic analysis reveal that the EMW-induced conductivity transition of the EM material occurred with remarkable rapidity, demonstrating a characteristic response time of 0.34 µs (Figs. 2e and S25). Under EMW exposure, the resistance transition times for the steel microfiber-EVA composite and copper microfiber-EVA composite are 0.35 μs and 0.25 μs, respectively (Fig. S26). This demonstrates that varying the type of conductive filler and polymer matrix enables the modulation of transition time, thereby facilitating faster or slower resistance transitions. It is noteworthy that the LED remains on after the electric transient is present for only a very short time, and the EMW disappears. As shown in Fig. S27, the low resistance state of the EM material will not change with time extension even after the EMW source is turned off.

The amplitude and rising edge of the EMWs significantly affect the EMW effect, which is evaluated by experiments shown in Fig. 2f–h. Since the EMWs are dynamic electromagnetic fields, we utilize a signal generator connected with two copper plates to provide the dynamic parallel electric fields (Fig. 2f). The induced voltage across the EM material, measured at various points within the central region between the plates, is consistent (Fig. S28). This uniformity confirms the homogeneity of the applied electric field. Such changing electric fields will offer electromagnetic fields as EMWs to activate the EMW effects. The resistance of the EM material is monitored to evaluate the degree of particle cohering based on the current and voltage in the circuit. In addition, to avoid resistance measurement errors caused by induced currents (0.9 μA, Fig. S29) and to ensure the accuracy of the experimental results, the resistance measurements are carried out after switching off the electromagnetic field. As shown in the inset of Fig. 2g, electric pulses from the signal generator provide different transient EM fields with varied amplitude (E) and rising time (τ). With a certain rising edge (τ) of the amplitude for EM fields at 500 ns, the R/R0 ratio is reduced when increasing the amplitude of EMWs from 100 V/cm to 750 V/cm. In this work, for R/R0, R is the real-time resistance, and R0 is the initial resistance of the EM material. Besides, with the same amplitude, the fast-rising edge (τ) provides a stronger EMW effect. For τ at 5 ns, a small amplitude (5 V/cm) can generate a significant resistance decrease (Fig. 2g, inset). While for large τ at 150 ns, a much higher amplitude (>400 V/cm) is required to activate the significant conductive network optimization. It should be noted that static electric fields will not be able to cohere the microfillers in polymers. As shown in Fig. S30, the resistance of the EM material does not change when applying static electric fields up to 750 V/cm for a sufficient time (>600 s). Actually, the faster-changing electric fields can induce a higher electric voltage in the conductors to break down the surface oxides among microfibers. According to Faraday’s law ε = dΦ/dt = A(dB/dt) (1), higher-frequency sinusoidal voltages exhibit a greater E, thereby generating stronger induced voltages. As shown in Fig. S31, when sinusoidal voltages of varying frequencies (50 and 500 kHz) but identical amplitudes are applied to the copper plates, higher-frequency electric fields induced higher-amplitude voltages in the EM material, thereby enhancing the efficacy of the EMW effect. The electric fields with low E/τ values (e.g., strong static electric fields with the greatest τ value) cannot excite the EMW effects due to the low induced voltage in the composites.

Similar to the earliest EMW detector in radio technology, such cohering of particles is only temporarily fixed, and the sample will recover to the high resistance state upon slight vibration. A reverse resistance change can be conveniently achieved when utilizing external ultra-small strain (<0.14%, 29 mN) to disturb the connected microfibers in the EM material, which can be further verified by the resistance recovery of the materials. Movie S3 and Fig. S32 show that slight vibrating of the sample treated by EMWs can retrieve the high resistance (recovery ratio: >99.99%) of the EM material. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) is used to investigate the relationship between the network recovery and the external force (Inset in Fig. 3a, initial spacing between the two fixtures is 1 cm) upon measuring the resistance change. Figure 3a shows that when the tensile strain is above 0.14%, the EM material (length: 15 mm, width: 10 mm) can have the reversible conductor-insulator transition. It should be noted that during the stretching process corresponding to the resistance recovery, no cracks are generated in the polymer, and the vibration disrupted the fragile micro-welded points between fibers through a physico-mechanical process, thereby altering their contact state. The reverse conductive network transition under external micro-force is also very fast, which can be achieved in 20 μs (Fig. 3b, the external force on the EM material is offered by a commercially available micro-vibrator controlled by square signals in Fig. S34). As a result, with the micro-vibrator (Figs. S33 and S34), the EM materials can be successfully applied as an electronic component. The electronic design is illustrated in Fig. 3b (inset). The EM material membrane can be fixed on the surface of the micro-vibrator. As shown in Fig. 3c, upon EMWs and a vibrator, the reversible insulator-conductor transition can be achieved. Considering the above enthralling characteristics, the EMW effect provides fantastic control over the conductive network, which can make substantial contributions to modern electronics. For example, similar to magnetoresistive materials20,21, a kind of colossal electromagnetic resistive material with an astonishing 99.99% resistance change (4 orders of magnitude change in resistance from above 50 MΩ to 1 kΩ) can be conveniently created (steel microfiber-SIS composite, Fig. 3d). This resistance variation remains remarkably stable beyond 104 on/off switching cycles, showing no significant change in baseline or peak-to-peak resistance values (Figs. 3e and S35). Moreover, the resistance switching state (on/off) of the EM material is flexibly tunable. By adjusting the frequency and amplitude of the control signal, the material’s resistance can maintain stable switching from above >5 MΩ to 1 kΩ over 104 cycles with a 3 s period during cycling (Figs. S34 and S36). Therefore, this work gives a fresh perspective on the field of future flexible resistive memory electronics. Figure 3f shows the typical electronic design for the EM materials to work as a resistive memory device with the capability of a rapid switch with multiple states. The EMWs for the sample work like the third electrode in the device, which can control the multiple resistive states remotely. Figure 3f (middle) and Fig. 3c have already indicated that EM materials can show rapid and stable on/off (0 or 1 states) features in electronics upon EMWs with high E/τ values. Interestingly, different from most previously reported resistive memory materials22–24, EMW effects can provide multiple resistive states that can be conveniently and remotely programmed by the E/τ values of EMWs (Fig. 3g, six different states, steel microfiber-SIS composite). These steps remain nearly constant over multiple cycles (Fig. S37), showing no signs of hysteresis or write fatigue. The different resistive states can be read through the current-voltage curves (Fig. S38, steel microfiber-SIS composite) in the circuit of the electronics. Figures 3h and S39 show one prototype experiment in which two EM materials are connected with the LEDs in series. Using EMWs, four states of “10”, “01”, “11”, and “00” can be easily and quickly produced and recorded. These prototype results strongly indicate that the EMW effect can be utilized to fabricate a type of resistive memory device. It should be noted that for samples or circuits asking for high spatial resolution or under electromagnetic shielding/interference, special efforts should be applied to realize the EMW effects. Currently, most magnetoresistive and resistive memory materials are based on rigid inorganic materials. This work provides such soft electronics based on flexible polymer composites that can be remotely controlled via EMWs.

More importantly, the optimized conductive network via the EMW effect can be permanently locked in the polymer composites if further treated by quick joule heating via transient voltage. As shown in Fig. 4a, steel fibers can be strongly cohered at the contact nodes by a transient voltage if the surface oxide has been broken down by the EMW effect. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 4b, a capacitor with a voltage of 100 V and a capacity of 3 μF is utilized to provide a transient voltage in a short time (165 μs) on the sample that has been treated with EMWs. The sample can be permanently locked in a low-resistive state without recovery. The micrographs (Figs. 4c and S40) clearly show the local cohering of steel microfibers encapsulated by polymer within the EM material. With the combined strategy of EMW and transient voltage treatment, the EM material shows permanently stable resistance, which can withstand the 1000 cyclic vibration tests as shown in Fig. 4d. To further investigate the stability of the cohered micro-filler network, long-term aging, temperature cycling, and strain testing are conducted. The integrally treated materials exhibit no detectable change in electrical resistance after 8 weeks (Fig. S41). Furthermore, the treated materials maintain a stable low-resistance state (<10 Ω, Fig. S42) across a temperature range of 25–120 °C. Fig. S43 additionally demonstrates that the processed composite retains its low-resistance state (below 1 kΩ) under 24.5% tensile strain. After the combined strategy treatment, the cohered micro-filler network exhibits unchanged mechanical and chemical stability following prolonged aging, thermal cycling, and mechanical stress application. In addition, it should be noted that the transient voltage via the capacitor is very important to guarantee the fast and high transient power for the local cohering. If using direct voltage (>30 V), it will burn the EM material (Fig. S44) due to the too long time (>1 s) of heating. While applying a transient low voltage (30 V), it will not generate high enough transient power for micro-cohering to lock the resistance permanently (EM material cannot withstand vibration testing, Figs. S45 and S46). It is well-known that the high loading value of expensive conductive fillers greatly increases the cost for the industry of composite materials. This combined strategy will show a heavy impact on the current electronic industry by offering a feasible and convenient way to lower the threshold value of the conductive composites. As shown in Fig. 4f, for steel microfibers as fillers, the conductive percolation threshold value after the combined treatment is almost one-third of that without the treatment (15 wt% vs 45 wt%), indicating a significant decrease in the demand for the conductive fillers. In addition, the impacts of filler size, distribution, and conductivity on the EMW effects are also investigated in detail, as shown in Figs. S47–S49. In addition, based on previous reports that carbon materials also exhibit the Branly effect19, combined with the experimental information of this work, collectively show that the composite treatment approach has broad applicability across different conductive filler systems, including carbon (carbon nanotube and graphene) and metal (copper powders) fillers. The electrical conductivity is significantly enhanced (2–4 magnitude) for all the composites with these fillers (Figs. 4g and S49–S51), suggesting a universal strategy for the current electronic industry. However, the composite with the graphene and graphene oxide hybrid is significantly greater than that observed in composites with the pristine graphene alone (Fig. S20). This again demonstrates that the surface oxide layers on carbon materials also play a crucial role in the EMW effects. Especially, costly silver particles are the most commonly used noble metal fillers for the electronic industry25–28. This work utilizes the simple shear mixing of silver particles (silver diameters: 1–1.5 μm) with resin to prepare the representative example for conductive polymer composites in electronics. With low silver usage (56 wt%), the electrical conductivity of the silver-resin composite after the combined treatment can achieve as high as 1.3 × 106 S/m (Figs. 4h, S52 and Table S2), surpassing most of the currently used silver-based composites in industry and academic research as electrical conductive paste, soft conductors, and electronic packaging materials8,29–43. In addition, the combined EMW strategy treatment can transition oxidation-prone silver-copper paste (65 wt%) from a non-conductive to a conductive state (8.0 × 103 S/m, Fig. S53). Such a strategy will undoubtedly alleviate the heavy cost for the current industry and meet the strict demands for most electronic applications.

Infrared photos were taken by an infrared thermal imaging thermometer (FLUKE TiS 20). The SEM images and EDS mapping were captured using an emission scanning electron microscope (FEI Inspect F50) equipped with EDS capabilities.

Preparation of metal-polymer composite: As shown in Fig. S1, the preparation of steel fiber-SIS composites with a 15 wt% mass fraction was taken as an example. SIS (4.00 g) and steel fibers (0.71 g) were shear-mixed in an open mill (STD-2KL) at 90 °C at 2 rad/s for 5 min to uniformly distribute the percolation network. The composite film with a thickness of 1 mm was then obtained by hot pressing at 120 °C for 2 min under 20 tonnes of pressure using a melt-compounder (AP2113, AUPLEX). To unite the standard of samples, the composite film was cut into identical rectangular samples (length: 30 mm ± 1 mm, width: 10 mm ± 1 mm, height: 1 mm). Copper electrodes (length: 13 cm, width: 10 mm) were attached to the ends of the samples for test standby as shown in Fig. S2. Copper electrodes were placed on the two ends of the rectangular sample 1 cm apart in the center. The copper electrodes were thermally bonded into rectangular samples at 120 °C for 2 min to ensure firm adhesion. Similarly, other samples with different fillers were prepared using the method described above.

Evaluation for the percolation network transition based on resistance change upon electromagnetic fields with different rising edges and amplitude: The main components in the experiment were steel microfiber—SIS composites, waveform generators, power amplifiers, two copper plates, and a multimeter. The waveform generator was connected to an amplifier. The signal from the waveform generator was modulated as a transient wave with a high level of 4 V, a low level of 0 V, a period of 1 s, and a duty cycle of 0.02%. The amplified signal was connected with wires to two parallel copper plates. The composite was connected to a multimeter and placed between parallel copper plates to format test circuit. Then, the rising edge and the signal from the waveform generator were controlled, and the amplification of the power amplifier was used to make the different maximum values of the electric field strength between parallel plates in the working circuit. The electric field between two copper plates was controlled from 0–750 V/cm. The falling edge of the signal was much larger (above 20 μs) than the rising edge (τ) to ensure a single fast pulse in one period. The modulation of the composite’s percolation network by different electric field strengths was evaluated by reading the change in resistance of the multimeter.

### Reviewer 2

Thank you so much for giving me a chance to review the manuscript entitled “Cohering Particles via Weak Electromagnetic Waves for Highly Conductive Polymer Composites”, submitted to Nat Comm. The authors present an intriguing and technically sound strategy for enhancing electrical conductivity in polymer composites via weak electromagnetic wave (EMW) stimulation - a concept inspired by the classical Branly effect.
The manuscript is well-structured and offers a compelling combination of historical context and modern application. I find the demonstration of EMW-induced coherence of conductive fillers along with its reversible and lockable conductivity transitions to be a significant and novel contribution, particularly in the context of flexible electronics and low-cost resistive memory design.
That said, I have raised several comments regarding the interpretation of the chemical and physical mechanisms and the clarity of data presentation in the figures. I believe addressing these points will further strengthen the quality and impact of the manuscript.
I appreciate the opportunity to contribute to the peer review process and would be happy to provide further input if needed.
Please see the comments below:
1. The induced voltage during EMW exposure is stated to arise from electric fields with high E/τ values, but what are the actual voltages generated across individual fiber junctions in the composites? Are these voltages directly measured or inferred? What modeling or simulation supports this?
2. The authors claim that Joule heating from transient voltages induced by EMWs is responsible for oxide breakdown and fiber cohering. However, is there any thermal imaging or time-resolved IR thermography to directly verify this localized heating? Could this be separated from general dielectric heating of the polymer?
3. While the breakdown of surface oxides is a central claim, are there any XPS, TEM, or EDS analyses performed on the fiber surfaces before and after EMW treatment to confirm oxide layer removal or alteration?
4. The setup employs parallel plates or localized EFB emitters. How uniform is the field within the composite? Could non-uniformity cause uneven cohering, creating hotspots or weak regions in the percolation network? Are cross-sectional conductivity maps or tomographic images available?
5. The response time of 0.34 µs is very fast. How was this time constant extracted—was it limited by the RC time of the measurement circuit or the intrinsic material switching? Can faster switching be achieved by optimizing filler distribution or polymer viscosity?
6. The resistance recovery upon strain is attributed to the mechanical separation of cohered fibers. Has this been confirmed by in-situ SEM or micro-CT under strain? Are cracks formed in the matrix or is the disconnection occurring only at the fiber-fiber contact?
7. The paper shows >10,000 switching cycles, but is there any degradation in peak-to-peak resistance or gradual baseline drift? Has the endurance been tested under different strain amplitudes or frequencies? This is critical for realistic flexible electronics applications.
8. The memory behavior with multiple states (Fig. 3g) shows discrete resistance steps. Is this scaling linear, logarithmic, or stochastic with respect to EMW amplitude or energy? Does this show any hysteresis or write fatigue over multiple cycles?
9. The work briefly shows various fillers (CNT, graphene, Cu particles), but how does filler aspect ratio, conductivity, and dispersion affect the EMW-induced transition? Are there statistical analyses comparing percolation thresholds and resistance change magnitudes across these systems?
10. The paper states that 10⁻⁶ mW EMW power is sufficient to trigger transitions. But what is the total energy input per activation event (considering pulse width, capacitor discharge, and delivery losses)? How does this compare to thermal sintering, photonic curing, or microwave treatments in terms of J/cm³?
11. How do the authors differentiate between the effects of EMW-induced electrical breakdown and electrostatic discharge or capacitive coupling artifacts?
12. To what extent has the electric field strength induced across microfibers been quantitatively verified or modeled (e.g., electric potential gradient, capacitive coupling, or field enhancement at fiber tips)?
13. Can the mechanical or chemical stability of the “cohered” microfiller networks be validated over time, temperature cycling, or mechanical strain, especially in the “permanent” state?
14. What are the potential limitations (e.g., shielding issues, spatial resolution, EM interference) of using EMWs as a remote and selective tool for device fabrication or activation in complex circuits?

2. The authors claim that Joule heating from transient voltages induced by EMWs is
responsible for oxide breakdown and fiber cohering. However, is there any thermal
imaging or time-resolved IR thermography to directly verify this localized heating?
Could this be separated from general dielectric heating of the polymer?
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful questions regarding the
local Joule heating mechanism. Regarding whether the Joule heat generated by the
transient voltage induced by EMW is the direct cause of oxide breakdown and fiber
adhesion, we fully understand the reviewers' concern that they expect to see direct
thermal imaging evidence.
The most critical challenge lies in the extremely high required temporal and spatial
resolution of IR camera. The response time of the conductivity change we observed
was only 0.34 μs (Fig. 2e). However, the frame rates of the currently most advanced
commercial high-speed infrared thermal imagers (such as FLIR X8500, Child window:
29,134 Hz, 64 × 4 pixels) are typically in the range of tens of thousands of hertz, and
the single-frame acquisition time is in the order of 10 microseconds, which is far from
sufficient to capture the sub-microsecond transient heating process. In addition, for
the local Joule heating, the size of the heated region on the microfibers (diameter: 12 -
22 μm) is usually in the nanoscale (as shown in Fig. 2a, the nanoscale breakdown
indentations). However, these most advanced IR thermal imagers usually have a
resolution of over 10 μm. Furthermore, there are also significant obstacles in terms of
spatial resolution. The polymer matrix (such as SIS rubber) has a strong absorption
and scattering effect on infrared signals, significantly attenuating the thermal radiation
signals from deep layers or tiny contact points. As a result, the weak signals of the
target hotspots are overwhelmed by background noise and the signals of the matrix.
We have tried different IR thermal imagers in our university. It is quite challenging to
observe the temperature difference within such a small region.
We acknowledge that, under the current technological conditions, there are significant
challenges in directly, in situ, and with high spatial and temporal resolution observing
the transient Joule heating process at the micro-nano level contact points within
composite materials. In previous studies (Journal de Physique III, 1997, 7, 303-310),
by directly visualizing (using infrared cameras) the conduction path when a single
layer of aluminum beads was subjected to high voltage, the phenomenon of
conduction transition could be observed. Therefore, to simulate the Joule heating
phenomenon by the transient induced voltage of EMW, we utilized a capacitor (3 μF)
to apply a pulsed voltage (fig. SD , 80 V, 412 μs; fig. SD , 200V, 425 μs) directly at
1 2
both ends of the composite material to enhance the phenomenon and facilitate
observation. As shown in fig. S16, as the voltage at both ends of the EM material
increases, the internal heat generated also significantly increases. It has been
confirmed that Joule heat is generated under the transient pulse voltage.
The conventional dielectric heating of polymers generates heat through molecular
friction, resulting in a uniform temperature rise throughout the material. The typical
timescale is on the order of seconds (Macromol. Rapid Commun. 2019, 40, 1800669;
ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2022, 14, 50215−50224). In this work, the surface oxide
layer on the conductive filler is induced to break down by a high-rate electromagnetic
field, causing an increase in temperature at the contact points. The typical timescale is
on the order of nanoseconds.

will be highlighted in yellow.

14. What are the potential limitations (e.g., shielding issues, spatial resolution, EM
interference) of using EMWs as a remote and selective tool for device fabrication or
activation in complex circuits?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising these critical limitations. When
implementing EMW technology as a remote selective tool in complex circuits, key
constraints include:
(1) Electromagnetic Shielding: Metallic enclosures or PCB copper layers (> 35 μm)
attenuate EM fields, acting as de facto Faraday cages. Mitigation: Localized
RF-transparent substrates (e.g., alumina ceramics) may reduce attenuation but require
thermal/mechanical validation.
(2) Spatial resolution: Since the EMWs generated by the EMW source are spatially
diffuse, it does not have spatial selectivity when acting on EM materials.
(3) Electromagnetic Interference (EMI): Fast-rise pulses (5–8 ns) exhibit significant
coupling to adjacent traces, risking digital switching errors and analog SNR
degradation. Mitigation: Localized shielding (Mu-metal enclosures) reduced crosstalk
in tests but increased form factor complexity.
These limitations and mitigation analyses have been incorporated into the manuscript,
with revisions highlighted in yellow.

2: "The mechanism of surface oxide breakdown and joule heating induced by EMWs
is not sufficiently explained. How exactly do weak EMWs (10⁻⁶ mW) generate
enough energy to break down oxide layers? What is the theoretical basis for the E/τ
ratio dependency, and why is this parameter critical for the EMW effect?"
Response: We would like to express our gratitude to the reviewer for the comments.
The core mechanism by which weak EMWs (10⁻⁶ mW) disrupt oxide layers lies in
the spatiotemporal concentration of energy at nanoscale contact points: Nanoscale
protrusions on metal microfiber surfaces (with curvature radii ≈ 50 nm) compress the
actual contact area to 10⁻¹²–10⁻¹⁰ m². This enables geometric field enhancement (β ≈
10³–10⁴) to locally amplify weak external fields (e.g., 20 V/cm) beyond 2×107 V/m
(Chem. Commun. 2025, 61, 9343-9358; Appl. Phys. Lett. 2006. 88. 104101).
Concurrently, the nanosecond-scale transient nature of EMWs (rise time τ ≈ 5 ns)
generates an induced voltage gradient (dV/dt ∝ E/τ) that produces instantaneous
power densities up to 10¹⁰ W/m³ at contact gaps. This value far exceeds the dielectric
breakdown threshold of the oxide layer. The resulting micro-arcs trigger localized
Joule heating within thermally confined zones (< 100 nm), where suppressed thermal
diffusion permits temperatures to surge transiently high, thereby achieving molten
welding at metallic contact points.
The ratio E/τ (electric field strength to perturbation time window) is critically
important for the EMW effect, as demonstrated both theoretically and experimentally.

work lies in the Branly effect, wherein conductive metal particles undergo cohering
under EMW exposure, substantially enhancing electrical conductivity. Branly
demonstrated this phenomenon using particles immobilized in wax or resin, proving
that particle displacement is unnecessary. Instead, conductive network reorganization
occurs exclusively through optimization of existing contact points without long-range
migration. EMWs induce localized oxide layer breakdown at filler contact interfaces,
followed by micro-weld formation via Joule heating-induced fusion, which resists
polymer elastic rebound.

## Paper

## Abstract

Highly electrically conductive polymer composites are fundamental materials for today’s electronic engineering. However, these composites are very expensive since heavy loading of costly conductive particles (fillers) is required to guarantee high electrical conductivity. This work successfully reports that weak electromagnetic waves (EMWs) could cohere the microparticles to optimize conductive networks for highly conductive polymer composites. Such an EMW strategy arises from the earliest EMW detector (coherer) invented by Marconi and Popov in 1895 via the breakdown of surface oxides and cohering of the micro-conductors by EMWs. The flexible composite (metal microfiber-polymer) shows a unique insulator-conductor transition with drastic resistance change (50 MΩ to 1 kΩ) under weak EMWs (power: 10-6 mW). The EMW strategy is extremely rapid (0.34 µs) and highly stable (104 cycles). Such EMW effect universally describes the interactions between EM fields and composite materials that are suitable for general conductors (e.g., carbon- and metal-fillers) and most polymers.

---

## Introduction

Electrically conductive polymer composites are the fundamental materials in today’s electronic engineering and are broadly applied as soft conductors, plastic electronic components (e.g., antistatic shielding cover), and electronic packaging materials due to their combined advantages of electrical conductivity, polymer flexibility, and interfacial bonding capability1–3. The current market for conductive polymer composites achieves as high as $4.4 billion per year in the electronic industry4,5. Although broadly utilized, the highly conductive composites are usually quite expensive since very high loading of costly fillers (usually beyond 75wt% for noble metal particles) is required to achieve sufficient conductive networks to guarantee good electrical performance3. Lots of investigations have been performed to lower the loading values to reduce the cost, including using specific fillers (silver nanowires, silver flakes, carbon fibers, and graphene) and unique blending strategies (solvent or bicontinuous phase assisted)6–9. However, these techniques or specific fillers are not prevalent in the industry due to the difficult synthesis, complicated steps, and strict requirements for the processing. So far, using a large quantity of costly conductive fillers in polymers is the most favored industrial method in electronics for high electrical conductivity in composites.

Electromagnetic waves (EMWs) have been the undoubted foundation for human society for more than 140 years since Hertz’s discovery in the 1880s10,11. The study of the interactions between EMWs and conductors is an important aspect of electromagnetics, yielding fruitful results for today’s technologies12. For example, radio technology uses EMWs and conductors to transmit signals, serving as the foundation of modern communication disciplines and making significant contribution to human society13,14. In the early history of radio technology, both Marconi and Popov utilized the interaction between metal powders and EMWs to receive EMWs as the earliest radio signal detector (coherer) in 189515. Such interaction is called the Branly effect, in which the high electrical resistive metal powders could be conveniently turned into low resistive materials by cohering the metal particles upon weak EMWs16,17. Although the coherer-type radio detector was quickly replaced by other advanced detectors due to the stability issue, the phenomenon between metals and EMWs strongly reminds us of a promising and convenient strategy to obtain highly conductive composites by low-energy EMWs.

In this work, we revisit the oldest EMW detector (coherer) from over a century ago and report a universal and convenient strategy that can cohere the conductive microfillers in polymers for highly electrically conductive composites through weak EMWs. Such an EMW effect arises from the Branly effect that can break down the thin oxides and then produce the joule heat from the induced voltage by EMWs to cohere the microfillers in polymers. Excitingly, applying weak EMW (power: 10−6 mW) on the composites remotely for a very short time (<1 µs) is sufficient to optimize the conductive network in the composites, leading to a significant change in material performance. The flexible metal microfiber polymer composite can have a unique insulator-conductor transition with a drastic resistance change in 4 orders of magnitude from 50 MΩ to 1 kΩ through emitting EMWs at a long distance (5 m). Systematic investigations in this work find that the EMW effect is heavily influenced by the amplitude and the rising/falling edge time of EMWs. Remarkably, the resistance transition is completely reversible (recovery ratio: ~100%) upon external micro-force (29 mN) and can withstand more than 104 cycles of such transition. It is worth noting that the EMW effect is a general strategy that universally describes the interactions between dynamic EM fields and conductors without strict requirements for metals and polymers. Flexible resistive memory devices with similar behaviors to magnetoresistive materials can be successfully and conveniently fabricated based on EMW effects. More importantly, different from the phenomena observed by Marconi and Popov, this work creatively finds that cohering of microfillers via EMWs could be permanently locked in the polymer composites if further treated by joule heating via transient voltage, which provides the electronic industry with a convenient strategy for highly conductive composites.

---

## Results

The composite in this work is prepared by simple shear mixing of metal micro-conductors (metal microfiber) and polymers (Figs. S1, S2 and Table S1). Styrene-Isoprene-Styrene (SIS) rubber (Mw: 30 kDa) is used as the polymer matrix since it shows high extensibility, while the metal microfibers in the work are steel fibers (SAE 316L, diameter: 12 μm and length: 500–800 μm, shown in Fig. S3) that are utilized as micro-fillers in polymer composites. In this work, unless specified, the EM materials refer to steel microfiber-SIS composite using SIS as a polymer matrix with 15 wt% above steel fibers (Fig. S4). Figure 1a, b show that emitting EMWs for a short time on a single metal microfiber will induce a high voltage between fibers. The induced voltage is also monitored (approximately 20 V, Figs. 1c and S5) when emitting the EMWs by an electrical fast burst (EFB) generator (Fig. S6) with a rising edge at 8 ns. Such induced voltage could produce a strong electric field strength (2.2 × 107 V/m based on the simulation of COMSOL Multiphysics, Fig. S7) among the fibers, exceeding the dielectric breakdown threshold of copper oxide18. The power-frequency spectrum of the EMWs is also recorded by the real-time spectrum analyzer (Fig. S8), which shows that the weak EMWs (power: 10−6 mW, triggered by EFB or piezoelectric ignitor with a total energy below 75 μJ) are sufficient to cohere the microfiber. Figure 1d exhibits that when the metal microfibers form composite materials with polymers, the microscopic breakdown of the surface oxide of microfibers in the polymer matrix before and after the EMW treatment will optimize the conductive network of the materials. Importantly, the EMW effect can be a general strategy that universally describes the microscopic interactions between EMWs and conductors. Figures S9–S13 and Table S1 demonstrate that other common conductors (such as copper particles, copper fibers, and carbon) and general polymers such as polycarbonate (PC), styrene-ethylene-butylene-styrene (SEBS), thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), low-density polyethylene (LDPE), ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA), and polylactic acid (PLA) show similar EMW effects.

The mechanism of the EMW effect for composites can be demonstrated by an old phenomenon reported over one century ago called the Branly effect. The Branly effect was used to construct the earliest radio signal detector (coherer) by Marconi and Popov via cohering metal powders upon weak EMWs. As shown in Fig. 2a1–a4, and 3D microscopic images (Fig. 2a3), after EMW (τ = 4 ns, Fig. S14) treatment, tiny dents are observed on the points where the steel beads (SAE 316L, Φ: 10 mm) contact. It indicates that EMWs can generate sufficiently high voltage between the steel beads, which will break down the surface oxide and cohere the metals through the induced voltage. To clearly observe such a cohering effect, a 2 kV transient voltage (500 µs, Fig. S15) is applied to the ends of the string with four contact beads. Due to the surface oxides of the beads, the string is electrically insulating. As shown in Fig. 2b, visible electric spark is generated among the four beads under the transient voltage, and the resistance is reduced to 3.8 Ω immediately. The four beads are cohered together at their joints (Fig. 2c) due to the local joule heating without dropping off upon lifting (inset in Fig. 2c). Building on this, copper fibers are positioned 1 cm away from the EMW source and treated for 20 s. As shown in Fig. S16, after EMW treatment, the surface at the contact point of the metal fibers is disrupted, leading to cohered fibers. These experimental results directly demonstrate the breakdown of the surface oxide layer on the microfibers. To further verify the transient heat for the composite sample under induced low voltage, a transient voltage (80 V, 412 μs) is applied across the EM material, and the resulting thermal effects are observed by an infrared camera (Fig. S17). The surface oxide breakdown and joule heating offer the efficient EMW effect for conductive microfillers in polymer composites. In addition, the previous report19 and information from prototype experiments in this work (Fig. S18) illustrate the Branly effect for pure carbon and metal fillers. EMW induces the insulator-to-conductor transition primarily through localized oxide layer breakdown and removal at the metal. As shown in the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) mapping (Fig. S19), after EMW treatment, the reduction of the O element (from 50.01 to 10.32%) in the energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) image of the treated oxidized copper surface directly demonstrates the removal of the oxide layer. In addition, samples with copper particles whose oxide layer is removed (Fig. S20) exhibited no such EMW effects. The surface oxide breakdown and joule heating offer the efficient EMW effect for conductive microfillers in polymer composites.

Figure 2d provides an intuitive view of the conductive network optimization upon measuring the electrical conductivity of the materials. Interestingly, similar to radio technology, EMW effects can be applied remotely (Fig. 2d). When EMWs are emitted at different distances from the sample (Movies S1, S2 and Figs. S21, S23), EM materials will show a unique insulator-conductor transition immediately. When EMWs are emitted at a distance of 5 m from the EM material, the composite exhibit a dramatic reduction in electrical resistance from >50 MΩ to 1 kΩ, and the lighting of the light-emitting diode (LED) is observed (Figs. 2d and S21–S23). EM materials are placed at various distances (0–6.6 m) from the EMW source to further investigate the influence of the EMW source-to-material distance on the EMW effect. As shown in Fig. S24, the effect attenuates exponentially with increasing distance from the EMW source. High-temporal-resolution measurements obtained through oscilloscopic analysis reveal that the EMW-induced conductivity transition of the EM material occurred with remarkable rapidity, demonstrating a characteristic response time of 0.34 µs (Figs. 2e and S25). Under EMW exposure, the resistance transition times for the steel microfiber-EVA composite and copper microfiber-EVA composite are 0.35 μs and 0.25 μs, respectively (Fig. S26). This demonstrates that varying the type of conductive filler and polymer matrix enables the modulation of transition time, thereby facilitating faster or slower resistance transitions. It is noteworthy that the LED remains on after the electric transient is present for only a very short time, and the EMW disappears. As shown in Fig. S27, the low resistance state of the EM material will not change with time extension even after the EMW source is turned off.

The amplitude and rising edge of the EMWs significantly affect the EMW effect, which is evaluated by experiments shown in Fig. 2f–h. Since the EMWs are dynamic electromagnetic fields, we utilize a signal generator connected with two copper plates to provide the dynamic parallel electric fields (Fig. 2f). The induced voltage across the EM material, measured at various points within the central region between the plates, is consistent (Fig. S28). This uniformity confirms the homogeneity of the applied electric field. Such changing electric fields will offer electromagnetic fields as EMWs to activate the EMW effects. The resistance of the EM material is monitored to evaluate the degree of particle cohering based on the current and voltage in the circuit. In addition, to avoid resistance measurement errors caused by induced currents (0.9 μA, Fig. S29) and to ensure the accuracy of the experimental results, the resistance measurements are carried out after switching off the electromagnetic field. As shown in the inset of Fig. 2g, electric pulses from the signal generator provide different transient EM fields with varied amplitude (E) and rising time (τ). With a certain rising edge (τ) of the amplitude for EM fields at 500 ns, the R/R0 ratio is reduced when increasing the amplitude of EMWs from 100 V/cm to 750 V/cm. In this work, for R/R0, R is the real-time resistance, and R0 is the initial resistance of the EM material. Besides, with the same amplitude, the fast-rising edge (τ) provides a stronger EMW effect. For τ at 5 ns, a small amplitude (5 V/cm) can generate a significant resistance decrease (Fig. 2g, inset). While for large τ at 150 ns, a much higher amplitude (>400 V/cm) is required to activate the significant conductive network optimization. It should be noted that static electric fields will not be able to cohere the microfillers in polymers. As shown in Fig. S30, the resistance of the EM material does not change when applying static electric fields up to 750 V/cm for a sufficient time (>600 s). Actually, the faster-changing electric fields can induce a higher electric voltage in the conductors to break down the surface oxides among microfibers. According to Faraday’s law ε = dΦ/dt = A(dB/dt) (1), higher-frequency sinusoidal voltages exhibit a greater E, thereby generating stronger induced voltages. As shown in Fig. S31, when sinusoidal voltages of varying frequencies (50 and 500 kHz) but identical amplitudes are applied to the copper plates, higher-frequency electric fields induced higher-amplitude voltages in the EM material, thereby enhancing the efficacy of the EMW effect. The electric fields with low E/τ values (e.g., strong static electric fields with the greatest τ value) cannot excite the EMW effects due to the low induced voltage in the composites.

Similar to the earliest EMW detector in radio technology, such cohering of particles is only temporarily fixed, and the sample will recover to the high resistance state upon slight vibration. A reverse resistance change can be conveniently achieved when utilizing external ultra-small strain (<0.14%, 29 mN) to disturb the connected microfibers in the EM material, which can be further verified by the resistance recovery of the materials. Movie S3 and Fig. S32 show that slight vibrating of the sample treated by EMWs can retrieve the high resistance (recovery ratio: >99.99%) of the EM material. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) is used to investigate the relationship between the network recovery and the external force (Inset in Fig. 3a, initial spacing between the two fixtures is 1 cm) upon measuring the resistance change. Figure 3a shows that when the tensile strain is above 0.14%, the EM material (length: 15 mm, width: 10 mm) can have the reversible conductor-insulator transition. It should be noted that during the stretching process corresponding to the resistance recovery, no cracks are generated in the polymer, and the vibration disrupted the fragile micro-welded points between fibers through a physico-mechanical process, thereby altering their contact state. The reverse conductive network transition under external micro-force is also very fast, which can be achieved in 20 μs (Fig. 3b, the external force on the EM material is offered by a commercially available micro-vibrator controlled by square signals in Fig. S34). As a result, with the micro-vibrator (Figs. S33 and S34), the EM materials can be successfully applied as an electronic component. The electronic design is illustrated in Fig. 3b (inset). The EM material membrane can be fixed on the surface of the micro-vibrator. As shown in Fig. 3c, upon EMWs and a vibrator, the reversible insulator-conductor transition can be achieved. Considering the above enthralling characteristics, the EMW effect provides fantastic control over the conductive network, which can make substantial contributions to modern electronics. For example, similar to magnetoresistive materials20,21, a kind of colossal electromagnetic resistive material with an astonishing 99.99% resistance change (4 orders of magnitude change in resistance from above 50 MΩ to 1 kΩ) can be conveniently created (steel microfiber-SIS composite, Fig. 3d). This resistance variation remains remarkably stable beyond 104 on/off switching cycles, showing no significant change in baseline or peak-to-peak resistance values (Figs. 3e and S35). Moreover, the resistance switching state (on/off) of the EM material is flexibly tunable. By adjusting the frequency and amplitude of the control signal, the material’s resistance can maintain stable switching from above >5 MΩ to 1 kΩ over 104 cycles with a 3 s period during cycling (Figs. S34 and S36). Therefore, this work gives a fresh perspective on the field of future flexible resistive memory electronics. Figure 3f shows the typical electronic design for the EM materials to work as a resistive memory device with the capability of a rapid switch with multiple states. The EMWs for the sample work like the third electrode in the device, which can control the multiple resistive states remotely. Figure 3f (middle) and Fig. 3c have already indicated that EM materials can show rapid and stable on/off (0 or 1 states) features in electronics upon EMWs with high E/τ values. Interestingly, different from most previously reported resistive memory materials22–24, EMW effects can provide multiple resistive states that can be conveniently and remotely programmed by the E/τ values of EMWs (Fig. 3g, six different states, steel microfiber-SIS composite). These steps remain nearly constant over multiple cycles (Fig. S37), showing no signs of hysteresis or write fatigue. The different resistive states can be read through the current-voltage curves (Fig. S38, steel microfiber-SIS composite) in the circuit of the electronics. Figures 3h and S39 show one prototype experiment in which two EM materials are connected with the LEDs in series. Using EMWs, four states of “10”, “01”, “11”, and “00” can be easily and quickly produced and recorded. These prototype results strongly indicate that the EMW effect can be utilized to fabricate a type of resistive memory device. It should be noted that for samples or circuits asking for high spatial resolution or under electromagnetic shielding/interference, special efforts should be applied to realize the EMW effects. Currently, most magnetoresistive and resistive memory materials are based on rigid inorganic materials. This work provides such soft electronics based on flexible polymer composites that can be remotely controlled via EMWs.

More importantly, the optimized conductive network via the EMW effect can be permanently locked in the polymer composites if further treated by quick joule heating via transient voltage. As shown in Fig. 4a, steel fibers can be strongly cohered at the contact nodes by a transient voltage if the surface oxide has been broken down by the EMW effect. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 4b, a capacitor with a voltage of 100 V and a capacity of 3 μF is utilized to provide a transient voltage in a short time (165 μs) on the sample that has been treated with EMWs. The sample can be permanently locked in a low-resistive state without recovery. The micrographs (Figs. 4c and S40) clearly show the local cohering of steel microfibers encapsulated by polymer within the EM material. With the combined strategy of EMW and transient voltage treatment, the EM material shows permanently stable resistance, which can withstand the 1000 cyclic vibration tests as shown in Fig. 4d. To further investigate the stability of the cohered micro-filler network, long-term aging, temperature cycling, and strain testing are conducted. The integrally treated materials exhibit no detectable change in electrical resistance after 8 weeks (Fig. S41). Furthermore, the treated materials maintain a stable low-resistance state (<10 Ω, Fig. S42) across a temperature range of 25–120 °C. Fig. S43 additionally demonstrates that the processed composite retains its low-resistance state (below 1 kΩ) under 24.5% tensile strain. After the combined strategy treatment, the cohered micro-filler network exhibits unchanged mechanical and chemical stability following prolonged aging, thermal cycling, and mechanical stress application. In addition, it should be noted that the transient voltage via the capacitor is very important to guarantee the fast and high transient power for the local cohering. If using direct voltage (>30 V), it will burn the EM material (Fig. S44) due to the too long time (>1 s) of heating. While applying a transient low voltage (30 V), it will not generate high enough transient power for micro-cohering to lock the resistance permanently (EM material cannot withstand vibration testing, Figs. S45 and S46). It is well-known that the high loading value of expensive conductive fillers greatly increases the cost for the industry of composite materials. This combined strategy will show a heavy impact on the current electronic industry by offering a feasible and convenient way to lower the threshold value of the conductive composites. As shown in Fig. 4f, for steel microfibers as fillers, the conductive percolation threshold value after the combined treatment is almost one-third of that without the treatment (15 wt% vs 45 wt%), indicating a significant decrease in the demand for the conductive fillers. In addition, the impacts of filler size, distribution, and conductivity on the EMW effects are also investigated in detail, as shown in Figs. S47–S49. In addition, based on previous reports that carbon materials also exhibit the Branly effect19, combined with the experimental information of this work, collectively show that the composite treatment approach has broad applicability across different conductive filler systems, including carbon (carbon nanotube and graphene) and metal (copper powders) fillers. The electrical conductivity is significantly enhanced (2–4 magnitude) for all the composites with these fillers (Figs. 4g and S49–S51), suggesting a universal strategy for the current electronic industry. However, the composite with the graphene and graphene oxide hybrid is significantly greater than that observed in composites with the pristine graphene alone (Fig. S20). This again demonstrates that the surface oxide layers on carbon materials also play a crucial role in the EMW effects. Especially, costly silver particles are the most commonly used noble metal fillers for the electronic industry25–28. This work utilizes the simple shear mixing of silver particles (silver diameters: 1–1.5 μm) with resin to prepare the representative example for conductive polymer composites in electronics. With low silver usage (56 wt%), the electrical conductivity of the silver-resin composite after the combined treatment can achieve as high as 1.3 × 106 S/m (Figs. 4h, S52 and Table S2), surpassing most of the currently used silver-based composites in industry and academic research as electrical conductive paste, soft conductors, and electronic packaging materials8,29–43. In addition, the combined EMW strategy treatment can transition oxidation-prone silver-copper paste (65 wt%) from a non-conductive to a conductive state (8.0 × 103 S/m, Fig. S53). Such a strategy will undoubtedly alleviate the heavy cost for the current industry and meet the strict demands for most electronic applications.

---

## Methods

Materials: Steel fibers (SAE 316L, Φ: 12 and 22 μm, length: 10 cm) and Copper fibers (T1, Φ: 22 μm) were purchased from Huitong New Materials Co., Ltd. Carbon nanotubes (CNT, Φ: 5–12 nm, length: 3–10 μm, 90–95%) were purchased from Wuxi Yifeng Technology Co., Ltd. Graphene oxide (GO, Φ: 20–40 μm, thickness: 1–10 nm, O: 40–45 wt%) was purchased from Nakate New Materials Co., Ltd. The few-layer graphene (Φ: 7–12 μm, 11–15 μm, diameter-thickness ratio: 9500, 98%) was purchased from Shenzhen Suiheng Graphene Technology Co. Steel beads (SAE 316L, Φ: 10 mm) were purchased from Glisen Hardware Co., Ltd. Silver powders (1 μm, 99.99%) were purchased from Exceed Technology (Suzhou) Co., Ltd. Conductive silver paste (50 wt%) was purchased from Suzhou Xinwei High-tech Material Co., Ltd. The silver-coated copper particles (Φ: 13 μm, 5 wt% silver content) were purchased from Jingrui Alloy Products Co., Ltd. Low-melting-point glass powder was purchased from Lingzhuo County Huachuan Mineral Products Processing Co., Ltd. The phenoxy resin (AR) was purchased from Shanghai Ron Chemical Technology Co., Ltd. Benzoyl Peroxide (BPO, AR) was purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. 2-(2-Butoxyethoxy)ethyl acetate (DBAC, 98%) was purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. SIS (YH-1105, 30 kDa) was purchased from Yoshida Chemical Co., Ltd. SEBS (YH-502) was purchased from Baling Petrochemical Co., Ltd. The Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS, Sylgard 184) was supplied by Dow Inc. PC (C-110, 30–100 kDa) was purchased from CHIMEI Co., Ltd. TPU (BTE-75A) was purchased from Risheng Chemical Co., Ltd. LDPE (1965P5) was purchased from Saudi Basic Industries Co. Ltd. EVA (40 W) was purchased from DuPont Co., Ltd., USA. The PLA (NatureWorks Ingeo 3260HP) was purchased from Dongguan Qisu & Plastic Materials Co., Ltd. Copper electrode (length: 5 m, width: 10 mm, height: 0.06 mm) was purchased from Shanghai Weitesi Electronic Technologies Co., Ltd. Piezoelectric ceramics (piezo ignitor, rising edge: 10–20 ns, amplitude: 10–50 kV). The micro-vibrators (DC 3–5 V) were purchased from the Jinhua Tuglisi Technology Co., Ltd.

Instruments: Metal micro-conductors (metal microfibers) and polymer were mixed by an open mill (STD-2KL) and a melt-compounder (AP2113, AUPLEX) to obtain the metal microfiber-polymer composite. EMWs were generated by the EFB generator (EFT61004TA, PR9240343897) and the piezoelectric ignitor. The power of the emitted EMWs at a distance of 5 cm from the emitting center was 10−6 mW, which was monitored by a real-time spectrum analyzer (SIGLENT SVA1032X) with an electric sensor (Fig. S8). Dynamic electromagnetic fields were generated by waveform generators (SIGLENT SDG1022X) and power amplifiers (ATA-2021B). The electrical resistance was measured by means of multimeters (VICTOR VC890C, Keysight 34461A, and Keithley DMM6500) and a precision four-point probe resistivity measurement system (HPS2663). The internal structure of the metal microfiber-polymer composite was observed by a digital microscope (Leica DVM6). The rising edge of the EMWs was measured by an oscillograph (UTD2152S-E). The response and recovery time for the metal microfiber-polymer composite upon EMWs and external micro-force was measured by an oscillograph (UTD2152S-E). The relationship between the network recovery and the external force upon measuring the resistance change was investigated by DMA (Discovery HR-20). The metal microfiber-polymer composites were stretched by an electro-mechanical stretching machine (E42.503, MTS Systems (China) Co., Ltd.). Infrared photos were taken by an infrared thermal imaging thermometer (FLUKE TiS 20). The SEM images and EDS mapping were captured using an emission scanning electron microscope (FEI Inspect F50) equipped with EDS capabilities.

Preparation of metal-polymer composite: As shown in Fig. S1, the preparation of steel fiber-SIS composites with a 15 wt% mass fraction was taken as an example. SIS (4.00 g) and steel fibers (0.71 g) were shear-mixed in an open mill (STD-2KL) at 90 °C at 2 rad/s for 5 min to uniformly distribute the percolation network. The composite film with a thickness of 1 mm was then obtained by hot pressing at 120 °C for 2 min under 20 tonnes of pressure using a melt-compounder (AP2113, AUPLEX). To unite the standard of samples, the composite film was cut into identical rectangular samples (length: 30 mm ± 1 mm, width: 10 mm ± 1 mm, height: 1 mm). Copper electrodes (length: 13 cm, width: 10 mm) were attached to the ends of the samples for test standby as shown in Fig. S2. Copper electrodes were placed on the two ends of the rectangular sample 1 cm apart in the center. The copper electrodes were thermally bonded into rectangular samples at 120 °C for 2 min to ensure firm adhesion. Similarly, other samples with different fillers were prepared using the method described above.

Evaluation for the percolation network transition based on resistance change upon electromagnetic fields with different rising edges and amplitude: The main components in the experiment were steel microfiber—SIS composites, waveform generators, power amplifiers, two copper plates, and a multimeter. The waveform generator was connected to an amplifier. The signal from the waveform generator was modulated as a transient wave with a high level of 4 V, a low level of 0 V, a period of 1 s, and a duty cycle of 0.02%. The amplified signal was connected with wires to two parallel copper plates. The composite was connected to a multimeter and placed between parallel copper plates to format test circuit. Then, the rising edge and the signal from the waveform generator were controlled, and the amplification of the power amplifier was used to make the different maximum values of the electric field strength between parallel plates in the working circuit. The electric field between two copper plates was controlled from 0–750 V/cm. The falling edge of the signal was much larger (above 20 μs) than the rising edge (τ) to ensure a single fast pulse in one period. The modulation of the composite’s percolation network by different electric field strengths was evaluated by reading the change in resistance of the multimeter.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this paper, the authors present a novel method for fabricating highly conductive composites by utilizing weak EMW to cohere the conductive microfillers in polymers. The rapidity and stability of the EMW strategy were quantitatively investigated. Meanwhile, flexible resistive memory devices with similar behaviors of magnetoresistive materials could be successfully and conveniently fabricated based on EMW effects. Furthermore, the authors demonstrated that microfibers can be permanently locked in the polymer composites under transient voltage. This EMW effect is applicable to common conductors and most polymers, offering a highly convenient strategy for developing high-conductivity polymer composites in electronic engineering. However, I don’t think this manuscript meets the publication criteria of Nature Communications because of the lack of physical significance. To enrich the impact of this work, I have some questions:
1. The steel bead experiment is used to illustrate the principle of the EMW effect, as show in Figure 2a-c. I suggest that the authors provide direct experimental results in the microscopic system. Please provide more experimental details, such as the frequency of EMW source on both microfiber composites and steel bead.
2. Does the distance between the EMW emission position and the sample location affect the conductive properties of the composite material? The study discusses scenarios with distances of 10 cm and 5 m, both of which can rapidly reduce the material's resistance to 1 kΩ. Does this imply that 5 m is not the maximum effective control distance?
3. Is the microscopic image in the inset of Figure 2d (upper right corner) taken after EMW irradiation? Please label it accordingly, and consider adding a microscopic image taken before EMW irradiation, as this would create a more pronounced contrast between the pre- and post-irradiation states.

Additionally, the R/R0 ratio is observed to decrease (not increase) when the amplitude of EMWs is raised from 100 V/cm to 750 V/cm. This discrepancy requires correction.
